28 A stationary sound wave is formed in a gas-filled tube of length L, which is closed at one end by a
piston. The length of the tube can be altered by moving the piston.
The length of the tube and the frequency of the sound are varied so that the stationary wave
always has two antinodes and two nodes, as shown.

hints: Notice the ends in the diagram: the open left end is a displacement antinode and the piston at the right end is a displacement node.
Count node-to-antinode spacings in length $L$: each adjacent node-antinode distance is $\lambda/4$, and this pattern with two nodes and two antinodes contains three such spacings.
Use $v = f\lambda$ with $\lambda$ from $L$, so $v$ depends on the product $fL$; read one clear point from the $f$ against $L$ in $\text{cm}$ curve and convert $L$ to $\text{m}$ before multiplying.
walkthrough: Identify the boundary conditions: open end at the left is an antinode, closed piston end at the right is a node, as shown by the wide envelope at the left and zero envelope at the piston.
Count quarter-wavelengths from left to right: antinode to node is $\lambda/4$, node to antinode is $\lambda/4$, antinode to node is $\lambda/4$, so $L = 3\lambda/4$.
Rearrange for wavelength: $\lambda = 4L/3$ and use the wave speed relation $v = f\lambda = 4fL/3$.

Read a convenient point on the $f$ against $L$ graph, for example $L = 15 \text{ cm} = 0.15 \text{ m}$ where $f \approx 1500 \text{ Hz}$, or $L = 10 \text{ cm} = 0.10 \text{ m}$ where $f \approx 2250 \text{ Hz}$.
Substitute with units: $v \approx 4 \times 1500 \times 0.15 / 3 = 300 \text{ m s}^{-1}$, with the $fL$ product constant along the hyperbola. This is option C.

A.explanation: Gives half the correct value, from using $\lambda = 2L/3$ instead of $4L/3$ for the three quarter-wavelengths in $L$.

B.explanation: Too low for $v = f\lambda$ with $\lambda = 4L/3$; it does not match $fL$ read from the $f$ against $L$ curve.

C.explanation: With $L = 3\lambda/4$ then $v = f\lambda = 4fL/3 \approx 300 \text{ m s}^{-1}$ from the graph.

D.explanation: Close to sound speed in air but too high for this gas; it would require a larger $fL$ product than the curve shows.
